slides.title: Review: pre-class reading
items: Last week, the thing that interrupted the CPU was a timer. Nearly everything we discussed in this context — the NVIC admitting the request, the vector table naming the handler, the ISR staying short, the volatile flag communicating with main() — was the interrupt mechanism, and none of it changes when we look at other interrupt sources.
Today we change only the interrupt source: we'll look at a pin triggering an interrupt.
This takes one new piece of hardware (the EXTI, between the pins and the NVIC) and four registers to configure it.
We'll also discover: when an ISR and main() both touch the same variable or register, "read it, change it, write it back" can silently lose an update.
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 2 min, including announcements. Safety line is on the wiring-check slide.

slides.title: Before any code: is the button still wired?
A counter with a button reset — one look per second
Watch the counter miss a press
What did the program miss?
slides.body:
A short tap sometimes resets the counter and sometimes does not; a press-and-hold always does. Why?

The program was inside delay_ms(), not looking. Polling reads a level, so it can only see a press that is still happening at the one instant it looks.

The solution: as we did with the timer, rather than have the program continuously check whether the button has been pressed, let the GPIO hardware alert the CPU when a press happens.

slides.title: Recap
items: A pin's interrupt goes through the EXTI first, because five ports of sixteen pins will not fit one NVIC line each.
Four switches, not Day 8's two: which port is on the line (EXTICR), which edge counts (FTSR1), whether the line is unmasked (IMR1), and the NVIC. Miss any one and there is no error and no interrupt.
Twelve lines share EXTI4_15_IRQHandler, so the handler reads FPR1 to learn which line fired — and clears it by writing 1, because the access type says rc_w1.
An ISR changing data main() also changes can lose an update silently. An ISR setting a flag cannot corrupt one — though two presses can still merge into one.
GPIOx->BSRR sets or clears a pin with a single write and no read, so there is no window for an interrupt to land in. It has no toggle.
Tonight: the same counter, with the delay replaced by a timer interrupt.
